opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because my own smart home setup is kind of a mess. I've got something like five different apps for lights, the thermostat, the blinds, the speakers, and each one has its own UI, its own account, its own idea of what a "room" is. It's very much software 1.0 thinking: someone hand-designed a bunch of screens and buttons, and you as the human have to learn their mental model.

What agents change is the interface layer. The natural interface to your home is just language, maybe plus a bit of context. "It's movie time." "I'm heading to bed." "Make it feel less like an office in here." These are fuzzy, high-level intents, and today you have to compile them by hand into twelve taps across four apps. An LLM is actually really good at that compilation step. It can take the intent, look at what devices exist and what state they're in, and figure out the sequence of actions.

So I think the software should be redesigned to be agent-first. Instead of the primary artifact being a glossy app, it should be a clean, well-documented API, a sort of "here's everything this device can do and here's its current state," written so an LLM can read it. Right now so much of this is locked behind apps where the only way in is clicking. I'd rather vendors ship something like a short text description of the device and its capabilities. The GUI becomes almost secondary, a debugging view.

But there are a few things I'd be careful about. First, this is the physical world, so the cost of mistakes is different. If the agent hallucinates in a chat, whatever. If it unlocks the front door or cranks the heat while you're on vacation, that's a real problem. So I'd want a tiered permission model. Lights and music, go ahead, low stakes. Locks, the garage, anything with safety implications, it should propose and I confirm. Kind of like how coding agents work well when they show you the diff before applying it.

Second, latency and reliability. When I flip a light switch I expect it to work in a hundred milliseconds, every single time. We can't regress on that just because there's an LLM in the loop. So I'd imagine a hybrid where the agent writes or updates routines and automations, the actual software 1.0 code that runs locally and deterministically, and it's not doing a big inference call every time you walk into the kitchen. The agent is more of the programmer of your home than the thing executing every single action.

And third, I'd love a lot of it to run locally. Your home is very intimate data: when you sleep, when you're away, who's over. I don't love the idea of all of that streaming to a cloud. Smaller models are getting quite capable, and this is a fairly constrained domain, so I think a local model that knows your house is very achievable.

Long term, the most interesting part is that it should just learn your preferences. You shouldn't have to configure anything. It notices you always dim the lights around ten, it asks, "Want me to just do this?" and you say yes. The home slowly programs itself around you. That's the version that actually feels like the future, as opposed to just a voice remote control bolted on top of the same old apps.

r001.rationale: It proposes replacing glossy, app-centered interfaces with a clean, documented API that agents can use directly, making the GUI secondary.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent translating a high-level intent into a sequence of actions across devices and four apps, enabling coordinated automations that a single app would not handle alone.

r003.rationale: It calls for agent-first software with APIs written for LLMs and frames the agent as the home’s programmer, making agents the intended users of the software.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the software people use for smart homes today is kind of a mess, and it's a mess for reasons that have nothing to do with the devices themselves. You have like twelve apps, each one from a different vendor, each with its own little UI, its own pairing flow, its own notion of a "scene" or a "routine." And the integration layer, the thing that's supposed to tie it all together, is this very brittle if-this-then-that programming that most people never actually set up because it's too much work. So the devices are capable, but the interface is the bottleneck.

And I think the way agents change this is that the app basically stops being the primary interface. The way I like to think about it is that the LLM becomes a kind of operating system layer, and the devices become peripherals. Right now you are the integration layer. You're the one who knows that the thermostat is a Nest and the lights are Hue and the lock is whatever, and you're the one who has to go click through each one. The agent can hold all of that context instead. You just say "I'm going to bed" or "we have guests coming Friday" and it figures out what that means in terms of the actual state of all the devices.

But I'd actually push back a little on the framing that it's just about voice or natural language replacing buttons. I think that's the shallow version. The more interesting thing is that these models can actually read the APIs. Like, the reason smart home integrations are so bad is that someone at a company has to sit down and write the adapter for every single device, and that's a huge amount of grunt work, so it never fully gets done. But an LLM can look at a device's API documentation, or even just poke at it, and figure out how to talk to it. So you go from this world where interoperability depends on standards bodies and partnerships to one where the agent just sort of... figures it out. That's a pretty big unlock.

The thing I'd be careful about, and I think about this a lot, is that you don't actually want a fully autonomous agent running your house. Not yet. These models are still kind of fallible in weird, non-human ways. They'll do nine things perfectly and then do something totally bizarre on the tenth. And in a smart home the failure modes are not trivial. It's your front door lock, it's your heating in winter, it's the garage. So I think the right design is this autonomy slider, where for low-stakes things, like the lights or the music, you just let it go, and for high-stakes things it proposes and you confirm. And over time, as trust builds and the models get better, you slide it further toward autonomous. You don't jump straight to the end.

The other piece I'd mention is that this is a place where the model should be running locally, or at least partially locally. Partly for privacy, obviously, because your home is about as personal as data gets. But also for latency and reliability. If your lights don't turn on because some cloud service is having an outage, that's a very bad user experience, and it's going to make people rightfully distrust the whole thing. So I think there's a real role for small, capable models on the edge that handle the routine stuff, with a bigger model you call out to when something is genuinely ambiguous.

So to sum it up, I think the shape of it is: fewer apps, more of a single conversational and increasingly ambient layer, agents that can learn to talk to devices without someone hand-writing every integration, a careful ramp on autonomy rather than a leap, and a lot of it running in the house rather than in a data center. That feels like the direction that actually makes the smart home deliver on what it's been promising for like fifteen years.

r001.rationale: It says the app stops being the primary interface and agents can read device APIs and figure out how to communicate with devices, describing an agent-facing API layer in place of vendor apps.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent using context across multiple devices to turn requests like “I'm going to bed” into coordinated device states, replacing brittle integrations that users rarely set up.

r003.rationale: The response presents agents as an interface and coordinator for people, but does not identify agents as the intended customers of software in an agent-first ecosystem.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is that software today assumes a human is going to operate it. So every smart home device comes with an app, and you have to find the right screen and remember where the setting is. You’re basically acting as the integration layer between all these devices.

With agents, I’d want the devices to expose capabilities that software can discover and use. What can you control? What’s the current state? What happens if you change it? Then I can say, “I’m going to bed,” and the agent can coordinate the lights, temperature, and locks without navigating five separate apps.

But I still want visibility and control. If it decides to change something, I should be able to see what it did, correct it, and undo it. And unlocking a door should have a different permission boundary from dimming a light. So I don’t think interfaces disappear. They become more about expressing intent, inspecting what’s happening, and stepping in when necessary.

r001.rationale: The response says devices should expose discoverable capabilities to agents, but it does not propose replacing dedicated apps with APIs; it explicitly says interfaces do not disappear.

r002.rationale: It says an agent could coordinate lights, temperature, and locks in response to “I’m going to bed,” without navigating five separate apps.

r003.rationale: The response describes an agent acting on a person’s intent, but does not identify agents acting on people’s behalf as the intended customers of software.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting shift is that you shouldn’t have to operate your home at the level of individual devices. Today you have an app for the lights, an app for the thermostat, and you’re basically the integration layer. You’re translating what you want into a sequence of button presses across all these interfaces.

With an agent, you could say, “I’m going to bed,” and it understands that this means checking the doors, adjusting the temperature, turning off some lights. But the underlying software has to make those actions available in a structured way. Having an AI poke around five different phone apps is a pretty awkward way to accomplish that.

And I’d still want a very good conventional interface. You want to see what the agent did, change your preferences, and override it immediately. If the lights are wrong, you shouldn’t have to have a conversation to turn them on. So I think the agent becomes this layer that coordinates things around your intent, while the software underneath makes the state and the controls really explicit.

r001.rationale: The response says the underlying software should expose actions in a structured way and calls an agent navigating multiple apps awkward, but it retains a conventional interface and does not propose replacing dedicated apps with APIs.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent coordinating doors, temperature, and lights in response to “I’m going to bed,” spanning controls that today sit in separate apps.

r003.rationale: The agent is described as coordinating actions around a person’s intent, but the response does not identify agents acting on people’s behalf as the intended customers of software.
